```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, comment = "##", fig.align = "center")
refresh_data <- FALSE
```

```{r packages, message = FALSE}
library(NNS)
packageVersion("NNS")
```

# Economic Variables

The variable list was used from the NY Fed Nowcast method
(<https://www.newyorkfed.org/research/policy/nowcast>) and augmented with
several additional variables, specifically:

* 10-year Treasury rates `DGS10`
* 2-10 year Treasury rate spread `T10Y2Y`
* weekly unemployment claims `ICSA`
* Federal Reserve total assets `WALCL`

```{r variables}
variables <- c(PAYEMS = "Payroll Employment", JTSJOL = "Job Openings",
               CPIAUCSL = "Consumer Price Index", DGORDER = "Durable Goods Orders",
               RSAFS = "Retail Sales", UNRATE = "Unemployment Rate",
               HOUST = "Housing Starts", INDPRO = "Industrial Production",
               DSPIC96 = "Real Disposable Personal Income", BOPTEXP = "Exports",
               BOPTIMP = "Imports", TTLCONS = "Construction Spending",
               IR = "Import Price Index", CPILFESL = "Core Consumer Price Index",
               PCEPILFE = "Core PCE Price Index", PCEPI = "PCE Price Index",
               PERMIT = "Building Permits", TCU = "Capacity Utilization Rate",
               BUSINV = "Business Inventories", ULCNFB = "Unit Labor Cost (quarterly)",
               IQ = "Export Price Index", GACDISA066MSFRBNY = "Empire State Mfg Index",
               GACDFSA066MSFRBPHI = "Philadelphia Fed Mfg Index",
               PCEC96 = "Real Consumption Spending", GDPC1 = "Real GDP (quarterly)",
               ICSA = "Weekly Unemployment Claims", DGS10 = "10-year Treasury Rate",
               T10Y2Y = "2-10 year Treasury Spread", WALCL = "Fed Total Assets (weekly)")
knitr::kable(data.frame(FRED = names(variables), Series = unname(variables)))
```

The series come from FRED. Monthly series are used as published. Daily and
weekly series keep each month's last observation, as `NNS.nowcast()` did.
Quarterly series sit in the first month of their quarter, with the other two
months missing. The panel runs from January 2007 to December 2022, the month
of the archived page; every series is observed from January 2007 (real
consumption spending, `PCEC96`, starts there in the current vintage). The
archived page started in 2000 and filled the years before a series began.

```{r data}
if (refresh_data) {
  months <- format(seq(as.Date("2007-01-01"), as.Date("2022-12-01"), by = "month"), "%Y-%m")
  panel <- data.frame(month = months, sapply(names(variables), function(id) {
    x <- read.csv(paste0("https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.csv?id=", id),
                  na.strings = ".")
    x <- x[!is.na(x[[2]]), ]
    last <- tapply(x[[2]], substr(x[[1]], 1, 7), function(v) v[length(v)])
    as.numeric(last[months])
  }), check.names = FALSE)
  write.csv(panel, "data/Causal_Inference_Amongst_Macroeconomic_Variables_fred.csv",
            row.names = FALSE)
}
panel <- read.csv("data/Causal_Inference_Amongst_Macroeconomic_Variables_fred.csv",
                  check.names = FALSE)
econ_variables <- ts(panel[, names(variables)], start = c(2007, 1), frequency = 12)
dim(econ_variables)
colSums(is.na(econ_variables))[colSums(is.na(econ_variables)) > 0]
```

# Step 1: Align the Frequencies with `NNS.VAR`

This preliminary step will create an interpolated/extrapolated data.frame of
all of the economic variables such that frequencies are aligned to monthly
values. `NNS.nowcast()` did this with the variables predefined; it called
`NNS.VAR` with `h = 0`, which returns just the completed data. Missing months
before a series' last observation are interpolated linearly; missing months
after it are `NNS.ARMA` forecasts (here November and December 2022 for the two
quarterly series).

```{r nowcast}
nns_estimates <- NNS.VAR(econ_variables, h = 0, tau = 12, nowcast = TRUE, status = FALSE)
# View the last year's values
tail(nns_estimates[, c("PAYEMS", "UNRATE", "GDPC1", "ULCNFB", "DGS10", "WALCL")], 12)
```

With `h = 0` no forecast is made, so the validation step of `NNS.VAR` does not run.
A forecast (`h > 0`) tunes on a chronological holdout whose predictors are
built from forecasts made at the holdout's origin (`validation = "pipeline"`).

# Step 2: Directional Association with `NNS.caus`

`NNS.caus(x, y, tau)` compares the lagged pairs $(x_{t-\tau}, y_t)$ and
$(y_{t-\tau}, x_t)$ after mapping each variable to the copula scale with its
ranks, so the result does not depend on units or on any increasing
transformation of either variable. For each direction it combines how much of
the effect's deviation is resolved by the candidate cause's position, $P$, with
the excess directional dependence of the lagged pair, $\rho$:

$$\tilde{C}_{x \to y} = \tfrac{1}{2}\left[P_{x \to y} + \max(\rho_{x \to y} - \rho_{y \to x}, 0)\right],
\qquad
C_{x \to y} = \frac{\tilde{C}_{x \to y} + \kappa}{\tilde{C}_{x \to y} + \tilde{C}_{y \to x} + 2\kappa},$$

with $\kappa = 1/\sqrt{n - \tau}$. The two directions sum to 1, and 0.5 means
no net direction. For a matrix, entry `[i, j]` is $C$(column `i` $\to$ column
`j`); the archived page read the matrix the other way round.

The index measures **directional lagged association**. It does not condition
on the effect's own history or on the other variables, and a common driver
that reaches one series before another can produce a direction without any
causal effect between them.

The permutation test below circularly shifts one series, which requires series
whose behaviour does not change over time. Levels of employment, prices or the
Fed's balance sheet trend upward, so each series is transformed first: monthly
log changes (percent) for positive trending series, monthly changes for rates,
and levels for the Treasury spread and the two survey indices.

```{r transform}
transform <- setNames(rep("log change", length(variables)), names(variables))
transform[c("UNRATE", "TCU", "DGS10")] <- "change"
transform[c("T10Y2Y", "GACDISA066MSFRBNY", "GACDFSA066MSFRBPHI")] <- "level"
X <- sapply(names(variables), function(id) {
  v <- nns_estimates[[id]]
  switch(transform[[id]],
         "log change" = c(NA, diff(log(v))) * 100,
         "change" = c(NA, diff(v)),
         "level" = v)
})
X <- X[-1, ]
rownames(X) <- rownames(nns_estimates)[-1]
table(transform)
```

We use a one-month lag, `tau = 1`.

```{r caus}
nns_econ_causes <- NNS.caus(X, tau = 1)
dim(nns_econ_causes)
```

Large 29x29 matrix output, so we will just call the `WALCL` row, the index of
`WALCL` leading each variable, and the matching column, each variable leading
`WALCL`.

```{r walcl}
walcl <- data.frame(`WALCL -> variable` = nns_econ_causes["WALCL", ],
                    `variable -> WALCL` = nns_econ_causes[, "WALCL"],
                    check.names = FALSE)[colnames(X) != "WALCL", ]
knitr::kable(walcl[order(-walcl[, 1]), ], digits = 3)
```

The `WALCL` row ranges from `r sprintf("%.2f", min(walcl[, 1]))` to
`r sprintf("%.2f", max(walcl[, 1]))`; `r sum(walcl[, 1] > 0.5)` of the 28
values are above 0.5. Distance from 0.5 alone is not evidence: the index
varies under independence too, more for persistent series. The next sections
calibrate it.

# Add Some Noise Terms

We will add some noise terms to see how `WALCL` relates to variables that, by
construction, it cannot lead. `NOISE` is $N(0,1)$ while `NOISE_2` is
$N(10,20)$. Because the index uses ranks, `NOISE_2` is a second noise draw on
another scale, nothing more.

```{r noise}
set.seed(123)
X_noise <- cbind(X, NOISE = rnorm(nrow(X), 0, 1), NOISE_2 = rnorm(nrow(X), 10, 20))
nns_econ_causes_with_noise <- NNS.caus(X_noise, tau = 1)
round(nns_econ_causes_with_noise[c("WALCL", "NOISE", "NOISE_2"), c("WALCL", "NOISE", "NOISE_2")], 3)
noise_rows <- c(nns_econ_causes_with_noise[c("NOISE", "NOISE_2"), colnames(X)])
round(summary(noise_rows), 3)
```

The noise rows' indices for the 29 economic variables run from
`r sprintf("%.2f", min(noise_rows))` to `r sprintf("%.2f", max(noise_rows))`,
against `r sprintf("%.2f", min(walcl[, 1]))` to
`r sprintf("%.2f", max(walcl[, 1]))` for the `WALCL` row.

# Significance and Strength of Inference

The archived page compared each `WALCL` value with the 95% quantile of
indices for 100 fresh draws of the noise terms. Independent noise has none of
the serial dependence of `WALCL`, so it is not a reference for `WALCL`.
`NNS.caus(..., p.value = TRUE)` instead shifts the effect series circularly
against `WALCL` by offsets at least `max(tau + 1, n / 10)` months from
alignment. The shift keeps each series' own dependence and breaks their
alignment; the p-values test the signed statistic $C_{x \to y} - C_{y \to x}$
against those shifts. The two noise series are included as a check.

```{r pvalues}
targets <- c(colnames(X)[colnames(X) != "WALCL"], "NOISE", "NOISE_2")
tests <- lapply(targets, function(v)
  NNS.caus(X_noise[, "WALCL"], X_noise[, v], tau = 1, p.value = TRUE, nperm = 1000, seed = 123))
final_comp <- data.frame(`WALCL -> variable` = sapply(tests, function(r) r$causation[[1]]),
                         `p (two-sided)` = sapply(tests, function(r) r$p.value$two.sided),
                         `p (WALCL leads)` = sapply(tests, function(r) r$p.value$x_causes_y),
                         row.names = targets, check.names = FALSE)
final_comp$`Holm p (two-sided)` <- NA
economic <- !(targets %in% c("NOISE", "NOISE_2"))
final_comp$`Holm p (two-sided)`[economic] <- p.adjust(final_comp$`p (two-sided)`[economic], "holm")
nperm_used <- tests[[1]]$p.value$nperm
knitr::kable(final_comp[order(final_comp$`p (two-sided)`), ], digits = 3)
```

Each test used the `r nperm_used` admissible shifts of
`r nrow(X) - 1` lagged pairs, so no p-value can be smaller than
`r sprintf("%.4f", 1 / (nperm_used + 1))`.

## Strength of Causal Inference

```{r strength}
below <- final_comp$`p (two-sided)` < 0.05
significant <- rownames(final_comp)[economic & below]
noise_below <- rownames(final_comp)[!economic & below]
knitr::kable(final_comp[below, , drop = FALSE], digits = 3)
```

```{r strength-text, include = FALSE}
listing <- function(v) if (length(v)) paste0(" (", paste(v, collapse = ", "), ")") else ""
holm_below <- sum(final_comp[["Holm p (two-sided)"]] < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Before adjustment, `r length(significant)` of the 28 economic
variables`r listing(significant)` and `r length(noise_below)` of the 2 noise
series`r listing(noise_below)` are below 5%. After a Holm adjustment for the 28
comparisons, `r if (holm_below == 0) "none is" else paste(holm_below, if (holm_below == 1) "is" else "are")`.
With 30 tests, one or two p-values below 5% are expected by chance alone, as
the noise check shows. A result here would describe a one-month directional
lagged association in 2007-2022, not an effect of the Fed's assets on the
economy.

> **Note (2026).** The archived page (December 2022) used `NNS.nowcast()`,
> which is no longer in `NNS`, applied the former `NNS.caus` to the variables'
> levels from 2000, read its matrix with the opposite orientation, and judged
> significance against independent noise. Its tables and its conclusion that
> Fed assets cause the listed variables are withdrawn. See
> `examples/example-corrections.md`.
